results.title: Statistics | Sensitivity, Specificity, PPV and NPV | Geeky Medics
results.content: The significant difference is that PPV and NPV use the **prevalence** of a condition to determine the likelihood of a test diagnosing **that specific disease.** Whereas sensitivity and specificity are **independent of prevalence.**. However, **a positive result would not mean they definitely have a UTI** because a highly specific test does **not** factor in **how common** **the disease is (prevalence)**. **Positive predictive value** (PPV) and **negative predictive value** (NPV) are directly related to **prevalence** and allow you to **clinically say how likely it is a patient has a specific disease**. The **positive predictive value** is the **probability** that following a **positive** **test** **result**, that individual will **truly** **have** that **specific** **disease**. The **negative predictive value** is the **probability** that following a **negative** **test** **result**, that individual will **truly not have that specific disease**. For any given test (i.e. sensitivity and specificity remain the same) **as prevalence decreases, the PPV decreases because there will be more false positives for every true positive**.

results.title: How does sensitivity relate to prevalence in choosing diagnostic tests?
results.content: # How does sensitivity relate to prevalence in choosing diagnostic tests? # Relationship Between Sensitivity, Prevalence, and Diagnostic Test Selection. **When choosing diagnostic tests, sensitivity should be prioritized in high-prevalence populations, while specificity becomes more important in low-prevalence populations due to their direct impact on predictive values and clinical decision-making.**. ## Understanding Sensitivity, Specificity and Prevalence. Sensitivity and specificity are fundamental characteristics of diagnostic tests with an inverse relationship between them:. Disease prevalence significantly impacts how these test characteristics translate to clinical utility:. Bayes' theorem directly connects prevalence to the clinical utility of test results:. * A test has higher positive predictive value in high-prevalence populations. * The same test has higher negative predictive value in low-prevalence populations 1. Consider a diagnostic test with 80% sensitivity and 80% specificity 1:. ## Practical Test Selection Based on Prevalence. 1. **Assuming fixed test characteristics**: Sensitivity and specificity can vary with disease severity, patient population, and test conditions 2, 3. 2. **Ignoring prevalence when interpreting results**: Even highly sensitive tests produce many false positives in low-prevalence settings 1. 3. **Workup bias**: When patients with positive tests are more likely to receive confirmatory testing, this inflates sensitivity and deflates specificity 1. 4. **Spectrum bias**: Tests often perform better in populations with more severe disease, which typically correlates with higher prevalence 4. 1. **Sequential testing**: Start with a highly sensitive test to rule out disease, then follow with a specific test to confirm diagnosis 2. 2. **Adjusting thresholds**: Consider modifying test cutoff values based on the clinical context and prevalence 1. By understanding how prevalence affects test performance, clinicians can select appropriate diagnostic tests that maximize clinical utility and minimize potential harms from misdiagnosis. results.title: What is Sensitivity, Specificity, False positive, False negative?
results.content: # What is Sensitivity, Specificity, False positive, False negative? When using known samples of a disease, sensitivity and specificity variables can be calculated for evaluation of the test and its results. * Sensitivity and specificity are independent of the population of interest subject to the tests while Positive predictive value (PPV) and negative predictive value (NPV) is used when considering the value of a test to a clinician and are dependent on the prevalence of the disease in the population of interest. * For example, a test that correctly identifies all positive samples in a panel is a very sensitive test while a test that only detects 80 % of the true positive samples and 20% of the samples are undetected, hence false negatives in the panel. This test will be termed to have a lower sensitivity because it is missing positives and having a false-negative rate (FPR). * To determine the sensitivity of a test probability (percentage) that a sample tests positive given that the patient has the disease,. * Therefore, a test with 100% specificity correctly identifies all patients without the disease, while a test with 80% specificity correctly reports 80% of patients without the disease as test negative (true negatives) but 20% patients without the disease are incorrectly identified as to test positive (false positives). Alternatively, subjecting patients to a test with high sensitivity and low specificity and a second test with low sensitivity and high specificity can identify all false positives and false negatives. * **SnNout**: A test with a high sensitivity value (**Sn**) that, when negative (**N**), helps to rule out a disease (**out**). * False-positive (test positive but are actually negative) = 15. * False-negative (test negative but are actually positive) =5. * Positive predictive value (PPV) is a probability value that a sample test positive is really positive while the negative predictive value (NPV) is the probability value that a sample test is really negative. * Therefore, it is correct to say that Sensitivity and specificity evaluate the test while PPV and NPV evaluate the results. * Therefore, if a test is positive, there is a 97% chance that it is correct and if the result is negative, there is a 95% chance it is correct.

results.title: Use of the MyProstateScore (MPS) Test to Rule Out ...
results.content: Thresholds were primarily assessed based on sensitivity (as opposed to NPV) given that NPV varies with outcome prevalence across cohorts.18,24 The threshold providing the optimal balance of sensitivity and negative test rate in the training cohort was applied to validation cohorts, and the sensitivity, specificity, NPV, and positive predictive value (PPV) were calculated.18,24 We calculated the number (%) of biopsies avoided, the number (%) of unnecessary biopsies (i.e. negative/GG1) avoided, and the number (%) of GG≥2 cancers missed if the threshold were used to select for biopsy.17 Analyses were performed in (i) the overall biopsy-referral population and (ii) the sub-population with PSA 3–10 ng/ml; or PSA<3 ng/ml with suspicious DRE, consistent with clinical guidelines (i.e. guideline-directed population).5 Test performance was assessed in clinically-pertinent subgroups, i.e. suspicious DRE25 and African-American (AA) men.26 Finally, validated numerical methods were used to demonstrate the clinically-based threshold model was statistically valid (Appendix).9,10 Analyses were performed using Stata IC v16.1 and R v3.6.1. The MyProstateScore test was previously demonstrated to significantly improve detection of GG≥2 cancer relative to PSA and the PCPT risk calculator.6 In the current analysis, we established and validated a MPS threshold based on the pressing clinical need to rule-out GG≥2 cancer in men referred for prostate biopsy. Previous studies have demonstrated improved overall predictive accuracy (i.e. area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC]) with stepwise addition of PCA3, T2:ERG, and the combined MPS model to PSA and the PCPT risk calculator.6 Furthermore, decision curve analysis revealed that use of MPS provided net clinical benefit relative to clinical models and reduced the number of biopsies performed,6 consistent with a recently-published clinical study.34 Still, the optimal testing approach in any clinical setting depends on several factors, including relative harm of false-negative and false-positive tests.8 The particular limitations of PSA and the landscape of cancer diagnosis are such that broad measures of performance (i.e. AUC) are less consequential, and “rule-in” tests (i.e. characterized by high specificity and PPV) are currently less attainable than a highly reliable rule-out test, which can practically reduce the population-wide burden secondary to PSA testing, while preserving detection of higher-grade cancers.
